selectionSummary: Selected for scale of cross-border effects, lasting institutional or economic significance, independent source coverage and contemporaneous November 6 developments: global AI-linked market losses, European threats against aviation and broadcasters, and EU platform-regulation action. This is an editorial judgment, not an objective top-three ranking.

snapshot.summary: A reassessment of AI capital spending spread through international stock markets; European aviation and media faced new anonymous security threats; and Brussels challenged TikTok's feed design in a preliminary regulatory case.
connections: All three events exposed vulnerabilities in transnational systems—capital markets, transport and information platforms—and the difficulty of weighing credible risk against premature conclusions.
Policy expectations and public confidence were consequential across financial, security and technology sectors, but reported fears did not establish their worst-case predictions.
uncertainties: The medium-term consequences for AI investment and world markets were not yet clear.
The authorship and coordination of Europe's threats were unverified.
The TikTok proceedings remained preliminary and contested at cutoff.

stories.title: AI-linked stock losses spread from Wall Street to Asian and European markets
stories.summary: Technology-share selling after Tuesday's US midterm elections spread across stock exchanges on Friday, with Japan's Nikkei falling almost 6% and South Korea's Kospi closing down 6.02% after an intraday circuit breaker. European stock indexes also weakened. Analysts tied the volatility partly to fears that a Democrat-controlled Congress and opposition to data-centre construction could restrain AI investment, while other observers considered the reaction excessive; US technology shares partially recovered Friday.
stories.whyItMatters: The repricing crosses borders through chip supply chains, pension investments and the financing of AI infrastructure. It tests whether exceptional capital spending on data centres can withstand political regulation and doubts about projected financial returns.
stories.region: Global / United States, East Asia and Europe
stories.selectionRationale: Sharp multi-continent asset moves, Asian circuit breakers, financing implications for a global technology industry and independently reported market data give the event unusually broad immediate economic reach. It is the stock-market aftermath of the US midterms, distinct from the election's institutional outcome.
stories.evidenceNote: Independent originating teams: Reuters Korean market reporters, Guardian UK business reporters and UOL's São Paulo newsroom. Reuters and UOL give matching Kospi close and circuit-breaker detail; Guardian independently documents the international spread. Causal attribution to election results reflects reported investor expectations, not proof that future legislation will curtail AI spending. Reuters original timestamp precedes its described close, indicating later updates without a visible precise update stamp.

South Korea's Kospi finished November 6 down 6.02% after a steeper intraday fall triggered a temporary trading halt.

stories.title: Another wave of threats disrupts European flights and broadcasters; culprits remain unidentified
stories.summary: New bomb warnings on November 6 affected passenger flights across Europe and forced security responses at Irish, British and Bulgarian broadcasters. One plane diverted to Venice and Hungarian jets escorted threatened commercial flights; Ireland's RTÉ evacuated its offices. Searches found no explosives, and no injuries were reported. Officials spoke of possible coordinated or hybrid disruption, but investigators had not established any perpetrator or government link.
stories.whyItMatters: False alarms can force diversions, air escorts and evacuations across multiple borders at modest cost to perpetrators. The episode exposes the difficulty of protecting transportation and media operations without overreacting to anonymous threats, amid concern about European infrastructure resilience.
stories.selectionRationale: Multi-country flight safety operations and threats to civilian broadcasters extend the consequences well beyond one jurisdiction; three direct and separately reported news accounts distinguish observed disruption from unconfirmed attribution.
stories.evidenceNote: AP original multi-country reporting, Reuters original cross-European bureau reporting and Guardian reporting from Dublin and elsewhere are separate originating newsrooms. AP's figure of 11 Friday threats versus Guardian's at least 18 affected flights reflect different counting units/updates; neither is silently merged into a single confirmed total. First publication of AP original is confirmed as Nov 6 by its dated independent distribution; AP site text itself omits a clear clock. The reported Russian and group associations are unproven.

stories.title: EU issues new preliminary TikTok findings over recommendation-system 'rabbit holes'
stories.summary: The European Commission on November 6 set out preliminary concerns under the Digital Services Act that TikTok's For You recommendations may repeatedly expose users, including minors, to harmful themes despite existing controls. Regulators demanded changes emphasizing stated user preferences and easier opt-outs; TikTok rejected the analysis as inaccurate and defended its safety measures. The proceedings were not a final finding of non-compliance, and possible penalties remained conditional.
stories.whyItMatters: The case targets the design of a major global recommendation engine rather than only individual videos. A final decision could affect how platforms rank material for millions of users and shape regulation, technical design choices and child-protection policies beyond Europe.
stories.selectionRationale: The EU is seeking potential redesign of an influential global recommendation system, with worldwide financial implications and direct child-safety impact. Three originating newsrooms independently describe the new regulatory step and the company's response.
stories.evidenceNote: AP original technology reporting by Kelvin Chan, Guardian original Brussels reporting by Jennifer Rankin and Euronews original signed reporting by Greta Ruffino (which cites AFP as an additional source, and obtained a company response directly) are independent originating stories. The Commission's assessment is described as preliminary and contested, not established harm or a final violation. AP exact original time is unavailable on its public publisher page; dated distribution confirms November 6.

commonFacts.text: On November 6 the European Commission set out new preliminary concerns under the Digital Services Act about TikTok's repetitive recommendation feed.
The Commission sought changes giving more weight to user preferences and more effective user controls over recommendations.
TikTok rejected the Commission's characterization, and the process had not yet produced a final non-compliance decision.

framingDifferences.text: The Guardian concentrates on vulnerable viewers, campaigners and risks to the engagement-based business model; Euronews emphasizes concrete feed redesign options and the firm's direct rebuttal.
AP emphasizes the procedural distinction between the preliminary charge and final sanctions; the Guardian explores the broader social and mental-health implications alleged by regulators.

uncertainties: Whether the Commission's preliminary findings would survive TikTok's response and lead to a fine or commitments was undecided on November 6.
The exact prevalence and causal magnitude of any mental-health harm from TikTok's recommendations were not independently established by these three reports.

unverifiedClaims.text: TikTok's algorithm had definitively caused the specific mental-health harms described in the Commission's case.
unverifiedClaims.reason: The Commission made preliminary risk findings that TikTok disputed; this edition does not convert disputed regulatory allegations into adjudicated scientific causation.
